entities.name: Malignant dysphagia
observations: Palliative management primarily concerns obstructing esophageal or gastroesophageal-junction cancer; urgency depends on oral intake, aspiration, dehydration, and airway risk.

entities.name: Covered SEMS
observations: Provides the fastest relief for severe malignant dysphagia and is favored when prognosis is short, performance status is poor, or immediate oral intake is needed.
Fully covered stents are more removable but migrate more; partially covered stents anchor better but may embed and be difficult to remove.
Covered SEMS are recommended for malignant tracheo-/broncho-esophageal fistula sealing.

entities.name: Brachytherapy
observations: In a 209-patient randomized trial, single-dose 12-Gy brachytherapy improved dysphagia more slowly than SEMS but achieved better long-term relief, fewer complications (21% vs 33%), less late hemorrhage (5% vs 13%), and better quality of life; survival did not differ.
Most attractive for patients with longer expected survival and access to specialist expertise.

entities.name: External-beam radiotherapy
observations: Can provide durable palliation but relief is delayed; it is a reasonable non-stent option when expected survival is more than approximately 3 months or broader tumor control is needed.
Concurrent external-beam radiotherapy with an esophageal stent is not recommended because of adverse-event concerns.

entities.name: Endoscopic debulking
observations: Dilation alone is usually transient and carries perforation risk; laser and photodynamic therapy are generally less favored because of adverse events, cost, or limited durability.

Selective debulking or ablation may help short focal intraluminal tumors or when stenting is unsuitable; repeat procedures are often needed. Cryotherapy remains promising but insufficiently established.

entities.name: Enteral nutrition
observations: Gastrostomy or jejunostomy is an important adjunct or alternative when luminal palliation is unsafe, ineffective, or inconsistent with goals; selection depends on anatomy, aspiration risk, prognosis, and planned treatment.
Before potentially curative therapy, feeding access is generally preferred to routine stenting.

entities.name: Curable esophageal cancer
observations: Routine stenting is generally inappropriate before surgery, neoadjuvant/perioperative therapy, or definitive chemoradiation; feeding access or carefully selected temporary alternatives are preferred.
The 2025 American Radium Society criteria rate stenting usually not appropriate in several curative-intent settings.

entities.name: PMID:15500894 Brachytherapy vs stent
observations: Randomized trial comparing single-dose 12-Gy brachytherapy with SEMS in 209 patients with inoperable esophageal or gastroesophageal-junction cancer found faster relief with SEMS but better long-term control and fewer complications with brachytherapy; survival was similar.

entities.name: PMID:27626318 ESGE guideline
observations: ESGE guidance supports covered SEMS for palliative malignant dysphagia, considers brachytherapy an alternative or adjunct in longer-surviving patients, recommends SEMS over laser/photodynamic therapy/bypass, and supports SEMS for malignant esophageal fistula sealing.

entities.name: PMID:40557604 ARS criteria
observations: 2025 American Radium Society Appropriate Use Criteria generally rate esophageal stenting as inappropriate in curative-intent settings and in locally recurrent disease within previously irradiated fields, while supporting selected fistula indications.
